title: Two Halves
concept: After this one you can see two people who share the three voices between them, and find the move that gives each of them all three.
bookIdea: A symbiosis is a relationship in which one person acts the Parent and the Adult while the other acts the Child, so between them they use only three of the six ego states.

opener.setting: Saturday, 7:40am. Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B, the kitchen. The fridge has a sheet on it in Maya's handwriting, and she has just come off a night shift.

lines.text: “Sam, the sheet says you still owe the gas. I've checked it twice.”
lines.cue: still in her ward shoes, not sitting down

lines.text: “I know, I know. I'm hopeless. You still love me, right?”
lines.cue: grinning at the fridge, already reaching for the biscuits

opener.ask: Which of them plays the Boss and the Pilot, which of them plays the Kid, and what move would give each of them all three voices?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Each line here comes from one of the three voices: the Boss, the Pilot or the Kid. Tap the voice that is talking, and then the picture of the pair.

items.text: She reads the week's jobs off the fridge sheet, one finger on each line, and does not look up. “Bins out Thursday. Gas by Friday. Don't argue, just do it.”
items.why: “Don't argue, just do it” is an order with no reasons and no room for a reply. That is the Boss, the voice that learned how a flat should run. The Pilot would give the facts and leave the choice open.

traps.1: The Pilot deals with what is in front of you, and the bins and the gas are that kind of fact. But the Pilot would not say “don't argue,” so the words here are more than facts.
traps.2: The Kid would whine or plead, something like “Oh, do I have to?” Maya is not asking for anything, so the Kid is not talking in this line.

items.example:
A school gate, Monday, 8:10am.
Mum: “Bag on your back. No dawdling. Don't argue.”
Son: “Okay.” He stops talking and walks to the gate with his eyes on the ground.

items.text: He holds up the empty milk carton and grins. “Sorry, sorry, I know, I'm hopeless. You love me anyway.” He reaches for the biscuit tin before anyone can answer.
items.why: The apology is charming, and it is also a way of collecting a warm nod without making a plan. “I'm hopeless” asks to be rescued, and the biscuit tin shows the wish is for comfort. That is the Kid, the part that wants a nod and asks for it.

traps.0: The Boss would be stern, something like “Pay it back today.” Sam is grinning and pleading, not giving orders, so the Boss is not the voice here.
traps.1: The Pilot would say what is owed and when it will be paid. Sam never mentions a date, and that missing date is the clue.

items.example:
A cricket net, Saturday.
Player: “Sorry, sorry, I dropped the catch again. You love me, right?”
Coach: “Fine. Go and get the ball, you clown.”

items.text: Maya keeps the sheet, counts every bill and tells Sam what to do. Sam keeps the jokes and the apologies, and waits to be told. The flat runs, and it runs on those two jobs only.
options: One plays the Boss and the Pilot, the other plays the Kid
A shared plan, with both of them checking the sheet
Two people who simply dislike chores
items.why: Maya gives the orders and does the sums, which are the Boss and the Pilot. Sam supplies the sorry and the charm, which is the Kid. Between them the flat uses three voices where two people could have six. That is the two halves pattern, and it stays stuck while each one keeps to their side.

traps.1: A shared plan would show both of them on the sheet. Here the sheet belongs to Maya alone, and Sam never opens it, so it only looks shared from across the room.
traps.2: Dislike of chores would be a feeling about the bins and the dishes. The clip is about how the two of them fit together, not about what they think of the work.

items.example:
A band with two players, Friday.
Drummer: “I've got the setlist and the van, and I'll tell you when to start. You just sing and keep everyone laughing.”
Singer: “Deal. And I'll forget the setlist, as usual.”

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Two scenes in the same flat. Maya plays the Boss and the Pilot, and Sam plays the Kid. Find the line that gives each of them a voice they have been leaving unused, and watch what the words do to the meters.

items.title: Monday, 22:30, the kitchen
items.setting: Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B. The sheet is on the fridge door in Maya's writing, and the light over the cooker is the only light on.

beats.text: “Sorry, sorry, I know. The rent's late again, and I'm the milk man of the month. I'll sort it, I promise.”
beats.cue: still in his work shirt, the milk carton in one hand

lines.text: “Tell me the day, Sam, not the promise. Friday, or Saturday?”
lines.outcome: He stops grinning for a second. “Friday. Put it on the sheet.”
lines.why: You ask for a date instead of accepting a sorry. A date is the Pilot's job, and Sam usually leaves the Pilot to Maya.

lines.text: “It's fine. Maya's already done the sheet.”
lines.outcome: He laughs, relieved. Then he goes to find the biscuits.
lines.why: It is kind, and it keeps the pattern as it is. Maya does the sheet, Sam does the sorry, and nobody has to plan anything.

lines.text: “You always say sorry and then nothing happens. We all know how this goes.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam puts the carton down, says “Right. Fine,” and goes to his room.
lines.why: You pick a side and hand Sam all of the blame. His warmth goes cold, and the sulk is all he has left to hold.

beats.text: “It's fine. I've done the sheet. Sam, you're down for the gas, and four hundred for the milk.”
beats.cue: standing at the counter in her scrubs, not sitting down

lines.text: “Maya, sit down first. Then show me the sheet, and we'll check the numbers together.”
lines.outcome: She hesitates, then pulls out a stool and sits with the sheet on her knee. “Fine. Check it, then.”
lines.why: You ask her to sit, which gives her the Kid's turn at being looked after, and you share the sums so the Pilot's job is no longer hers alone.

lines.text: “Thanks. Send me my share and I'll check it.”
lines.outcome: She nods and goes back to the cooker, the sheet still in her hand.
lines.why: It is polite and fair, but it leaves her on her feet doing the work alone. The pattern holds.

lines.text: “You're the only one who ever gets things done in this flat. I'd be lost without you.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Maya says “Sure, I'll keep doing it,” and turns back to the cooker.
lines.why: Praise like this ties her down. It makes the sheet hers and the applause yours, so she keeps the Boss's job and you keep the job of being impressed.

beats.text: “You're amazing, Maya. I don't know what we'd do without you.”

lines.text: “Then pay her on Friday, and she won't have to chase you for it.”
lines.outcome: The grin slips, then comes back smaller. “Friday. Yes. Okay.”
lines.why: You turn the praise into a plan. Praise with no date is a nod for being, and this one needs a Friday to count for anything.

lines.text: “No worries. It's what we do.”
lines.outcome: They both laugh, and the sheet stays exactly where it is.
lines.why: It sounds friendly, but it agrees that the pattern is normal. The praise is taken, and the sheet stays with Maya.

lines.text: “Then stop being late and she won't have to do the sheet at all.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam looks at the floor, Maya says “Don't, please,” and the room goes quiet.
lines.why: You blame Sam for both the lateness and the work, which splits the flat into two sides. It sounds fair, and it keeps everyone in the same seats.

beats.text: “Please don't make it a whole thing. I'm fine.”
beats.cue: rubbing her eyes with the heel of one hand

lines.text: “You're not fine if you're on your feet at ten at night. Sit, I'll make the tea, and we'll do the sheet after.”
lines.outcome: She sits. “Okay. Two sugars, and no sheet tonight.”
lines.why: You name the real feeling, which is tiredness, and you ask her to take a turn at being looked after. That is the Kid's voice, and she is allowed to use it.

lines.text: “OK. Goodnight, then. See you in the morning.”
lines.outcome: She says “Night,” and the sheet stays on the counter.
lines.why: A polite goodnight does no harm, but it leaves her on her feet with the sheet still undone.

lines.text: “Fine. You're always fine, aren't you? Nothing ever gets to you.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Maya puts the sheet in her pocket and goes to her room.
lines.why: This is a hook with a joke on the outside. It makes her steadiness the thing to prove, so she has to keep being the one who holds everything.

beats.text: “Shall I take the bins on Thursdays? I'll put it in my phone. I promise I will.”
beats.cue: already holding his phone, thumb over the calendar

lines.text: “Yes. Put it in the shared calendar, and tell Maya when it's done, not when she asks.”
lines.outcome: He types it in and grins. “Thursday, bins. I'll tell her when it's done.”
lines.why: You give Sam a plan he owns, and a report to make, so the planning starts to be his as well. That is the Pilot's job, which he usually hands away.

lines.text: “Sure. Thanks.”
lines.outcome: He pockets the phone. The bins will be done when someone else remembers them.
lines.why: You accept the offer but never ask for a plan, so it stays a feeling. Sure is polite, and the calendar stays empty.

lines.text: “Don't bother. You'll forget, and then it'll be on me again.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam puts the phone away and says nothing at all.
lines.why: This is blame again, and it tells him his offer does not count. He will stop offering, and the planning falls back on Maya.

items.payoff: Monday, 22:50. The milk is still on the counter, and the sheet on the fridge has not been checked.

fallout.them: Sam stops saying sorry in the flat for the rest of the week, and he does not offer anything else either.

items.title: Saturday, 7:40am, the kitchen
items.setting: Apartment 3B. Maya has come off a night shift, and the shopping list is on the table in her handwriting. Sam has his tote bag over one shoulder.

beats.text: “Shopping! Leave it to me. I'll get the good cheese and the mangoes. No list needed.”
beats.cue: already at the door with the tote bag over one shoulder

lines.text: “Do the list first, read it back to Maya, and then go for the mangoes.”
lines.outcome: He pulls out his phone and types. “Cheese, rice, mangoes last. Got it.”
lines.why: You turn his charm into a plan he reads back out loud, so he uses his Pilot as well as his warmth.

lines.text: “Nice one. Have fun. Bring back something sweet.”
lines.outcome: He grins and waves the tote bag. “Mangoes it is.”
lines.why: This is pleasant, but it gives Sam the fun part of the errand and leaves the list with Maya, who has been up all night.

lines.text: “Last time you came back with three tubs of ice cream and no rice. Don't do it again.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam says “Right, of course,” and goes out without the bag.
lines.why: Teasing him back into the Kid's corner shuts him out of the plan. The list stays on the table, unread.

beats.text: “I've written the list. Don't change it, it's already been checked twice.”
beats.cue: sitting at the table with a cup of tea she has not touched

lines.text: “Read it to me, and tell me which bit you'd like to hand over. The mangoes, maybe?”
lines.outcome: She looks up, surprised. “The mangoes. Yes. Okay.” She hands him the pen.
lines.why: You ask her to choose what to give away, instead of carrying the whole list alone. Giving a piece away lets her sit still while someone else does a bit of the Pilot's work.

lines.text: “OK, I'll stick to it exactly.”
lines.outcome: She nods, and the list stays where it is, all in her handwriting.
lines.why: Sticking to the list is fair, but it leaves the list with her and gives her no turn at being looked after.

lines.text: “It's your list, so if it's wrong, that's your fault and not mine.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Maya looks at the list, then at the door, and says nothing.
lines.why: This is blame, and it moves her from planning into a fight about the list. Now the list is the thing they argue about, and nothing gets bought.

beats.text: “I'll cook dinner as well. Lentils, or that potato one you like.”
beats.cue: bag back on his shoulder, already thinking about dinner

lines.text: “Lentils, and you own the rice timing, because you're better at it. Set a timer, and tell her when it's on.”
lines.outcome: He nods, pleased to be trusted with something specific. “Timer. Got it.”
lines.why: You give him a job with a clear end. He keeps his warmth and takes on the planning part of dinner.

lines.text: “Lovely. Surprise us.”
lines.outcome: He grins. “Surprise, I can do that.”
lines.why: This is warm and light. But a surprise dinner is a feeling with no plan, so Maya will still be checking the pot later.

lines.text: “You'll burn it like last time, so I'll cook it instead.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam's grin drops. “Fine. You do it, then.”
lines.why: You take the job from him before he has started. It looks like a rescue, and it keeps him in the Kid's corner for good.

beats.text: “I can't do the rest of the week like this. I'm so tired I can't tell what I'm saying.”
beats.cue: head against the cupboard door, eyes shut

lines.text: “That's true, and it's a lot. What would make Wednesday lighter, and who could take part of it?”
lines.outcome: She opens her eyes. “Wednesday's the bins and the laundry. Sam could do the bins.”
lines.why: You take her tiredness as real information and ask for a plan. She can be frank about the load, and the load gets a second pair of hands.

lines.text: “Don't worry, we'll sort it. Go to bed.”
lines.outcome: She says “We won't, we never do,” and goes to her room.
lines.why: This sounds like kindness, but it is a promise nobody makes. It takes the load off her for a minute and leaves the week as it was.

lines.text: “You always say you're tired. Make a plan or stop complaining.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Maya says “Fine,” and the tiredness goes back inside her.
lines.why: This is the Boss voice, and it shames the feeling without giving her a job. She goes back to carrying everything alone.

beats.text: “I'll do the bins on Wednesday, and I'll put the rent sheet on the fridge with my name on it.”
beats.cue: a little more serious now, the tote bag on the floor

lines.text: “Good. Write both on the sheet, and say them to Maya before you go out.”
lines.outcome: He writes it on the sheet. “Bins Wednesday, rent sheet, my name. Done.”
lines.why: You make his plan visible and have him say it out loud, so both of them can see it. Sam starts to use a voice he usually leaves to Maya.

lines.text: “Brilliant, you're a legend. Thank you.”
lines.outcome: He beams, and the plan goes back into a feeling.
lines.why: Praise is a warm nod, but it lands on the feeling and skips the plan. Nothing gets written down.

lines.text: “Don't promise. You never do it.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Sam picks up his bag and leaves, and the sheet stays blank.
lines.why: Calling it a promise you never keep sends him back to the Kid's corner, and it makes the plan something to doubt before it starts.

items.payoff: Saturday, 8:20am. The list stays on the table, and the shopping turns into a rushed trip to the corner shop.

fallout.you: Maya takes the list to her room and does the shopping herself, alone, in a hurry.

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Two questions to explain back. You can use the book words now.

items.text: “Maya keeps the sheet and gives the orders, and Sam keeps the jokes and waits to be told. Which word do the books use for a relationship where one person plays the Parent and the Adult and the other plays the Child?”
items.cue: turning her cup, one eyebrow up
items.why: Maya plays the Parent and the Adult, with the orders and the sums, and Sam plays the Child, with the sorry and the charm. Between them they use three of the six ego states. The books call that pattern a symbiosis.

traps.1: A racket is a stand-in feeling, something shown because the real one was not allowed. Sam's apologies might look like that, but the question is about the fit between two people, not about one feeling.
traps.2: Passivity describes one person's way of dodging a problem. Both of them act all the time, and the question asks how the two of them fit together.

items.example:
A school trip, Friday.
Teacher: “I've got the register and the bus times. You just smile at the parents.”
Helper: “Fine, I'll smile. Don't ask me about the bus.”

items.text: “What move would give both of them all three voices, the Boss, the Pilot and the Kid?”
options: Give Maya a turn at being looked after, and give Sam one piece of the planning with a clear hand-off.
Take over the sheet yourself, so neither of them has to think about it any more.
Tell Sam to stop apologising, since the apologies are wearing everyone out.
items.why: Both of them are using only part of what they have. Maya gets a turn in the Kid's chair, and Sam gets a piece of the Pilot's work with a clear end. That loosens the symbiosis from both ends without cutting anyone out of the flat.

traps.1: Taking over the sheet makes you the new Boss and Pilot, and the pair gets a third person to lean on. It feels helpful, but now the symbiosis includes you and nobody has taken up a new voice.
traps.2: Telling Sam to stop apologising cuts off his Kid without giving him a plan. It looks like a fix, and it leaves Maya with the whole sheet.

items.example:
A housing society meeting, Sunday.
Neighbour A: “I'll write the minutes, and you do the chairs and the tea, as always.”
Neighbour B: “Fine. You write, and one of us can sit down for a change. Me first.”

debrief.nadia: Two people in one flat, and a sheet on the fridge that only one of them ever looked at. Maya played the Boss and the Pilot and Sam played the Kid, so the flat used three voices where six were on offer. Give each of them a job from the voices they have been leaving to the other.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this symbiosis: a relationship in which one person acts the Parent and the Adult and the other acts the Child, so that between them they use only three of the six ego states.

reflection.prompt: In which relationship of yours does one person give the orders and do the sums while the other is looked after, and which one job could you take back this week?
